candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — implanted venous port access
candidate.educational_objective: Safely access an implanted venous port using appropriate skin antisepsis, aseptic technique, and a sterile non-coring (Huber) needle designed for the port septum.

options.A: Use a sterile non-coring (Huber) needle after appropriate site antisepsis and maintain aseptic port-access technique
options.B: Use a standard hypodermic needle because any sharp needle can safely penetrate the port septum
options.C: Use a peripheral IV catheter through the port septum to avoid a needle
options.D: Access the port without skin antisepsis when the overlying skin appears clean

candidate.rationale: FDA device classification identifies the sterile non-coring (Huber) needle as the needle used to access a subcutaneous implanted intravascular infusion port; its tip is designed to enter the septum without damaging it. CDC oncology infection-control guidance directs clinicians to perform hand hygiene, cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, and insert a non-coring needle while maintaining aseptic access technique. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Implanted venous ports are accessed with a sterile non-coring Huber needle after antisepsis using aseptic technique.
candidate.source_document_title: FDA Product Classification — Device non-coring (Huber) needle; Basic Infection Control and Prevention Plan for Outpatient Oncology Settings
